title: StockCountChanged
description:
A complete snapshot of a stock count's business-unit record as persisted at the moment of publish. Not a delta, not a patch, and never a list of changed field names — a consumer that missed earlier messages can act on any single message alone.

WHEN THIS FIRES. Two occasions, distinguished by the `Event-Type` message attribute, never by the payload:
  - `STOCK_COUNT_CREATED` — a stock count's business-unit record is created, on every creation path, including counts generated by the recurring stock-count scheduler.
  - `STOCK_COUNT_UPDATED` — a persisted edit changes `startDate`, `type` or `status`.
An edit that touches none of those three still carries the whole record if it publishes; the payload is always the full snapshot.

THE TWO IDS. `recordId` and `parentStockCountId` are both always present, even when they hold the same value, which they do on every single-business-unit creation path. That is deliberate: a consumer never has to infer which of the two a bare id refers to.

MESSAGE ATTRIBUTES. `Event-Type` is the discriminator and is an ATTRIBUTE, not a payload field, so a subscription can filter server-side without deserializing the body — for example `filter: 'attributes.Event-Type = "STOCK_COUNT_CREATED"'`. Its permitted values are exactly `STOCK_COUNT_CREATED` and `STOCK_COUNT_UPDATED`; it is never a constant such as `STOCK_COUNT_CHANGED`, never missing and never empty. Every message additionally carries `Tenant-Id`, `Business-Unit-Id`, `Stock-Count-Id` and `Correlation-Id` attributes; routing context is read from attributes and never from the body. `Stock-Count-Id` equals the `recordId` payload field, not `parentStockCountId`. On a scheduled-job publish, `Correlation-Id` is a job-scoped identifier shared by the messages that run publishes for the same tenant and business unit.

ORDERING. The topic is consumed with message ordering enabled and the publisher sets a real Pub/Sub ordering key of `{tenantId}-{businessUnitId}-{recordId}`, so messages for one record arrive in publish order.

STALE REPLAYS. `modifiedDatetime` is the producer's own write time and is present on every message of both event types. Ordering keys give FIFO for new messages only: a dead-lettered message unblocks its key, later messages process, and a DLQ replay can re-inject the stale one afterwards. Compare `modifiedDatetime` against the state you have already applied and discard anything older.

TIMESTAMP PRECISION — MILLISECONDS. All three timestamp fields on this topic (`modifiedDatetime`, `startDate`, `dueDate`) carry EXACTLY three fractional-second digits in UTC, e.g. `2026-09-02T10:39:30.076Z`. This is a contract guarantee, not an accident of the producer: both publish paths normalise through `getTime()`, because they previously disagreed — the create path emitted the Spanner commit response at 3 digits while the update path emitted a `PreciseDate` read-back at 9 digits, and those two widths do not sort as strings (`'.076348000Z' < '.076Z'`, since `'3' < 'Z'`). A consumer writing the obvious string comparison would have discarded the NEWER message and kept the stale one, defeating the very purpose of this field. A lexicographic string compare on `modifiedDatetime` is therefore safe on this topic. Do NOT assume the same of every topic in this estate: `grc.public.event.delivery-changed.v1` deliberately carries NINE fractional digits, because its payload comes from a single read-back row through one builder and is internally consistent at that width. The two topics differ on purpose; do not normalise one to the other.

businessUnitId.description: Id of the business unit this record belongs to

recordId.description: The business-unit-level record's own id (stock_count_business_units.record_id). Present even when equal to parentStockCountId, which it is on every single-business-unit creation path. The Stock-Count-Id message attribute equals this field

parentStockCountId.description: Id of the parent stock_counts row this business-unit record belongs to (stock_count_business_units.id). Present even when equal to recordId, so a consumer never has to infer which id it holds

status.description: Status of the stock count's business-unit record at the moment of publish

startDate.description: The day the count becomes active, as an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp at midnight. Millisecond precision: exactly three fractional-second digits, UTC. Every timestamp on this topic is normalised through getTime() on both publish paths, so the create path (Spanner commit response) and the update path (a PreciseDate read-back) cannot emit different widths. Sub-millisecond precision is dropped deliberately

dueDate.description: The day the count is due, as an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp at midnight. The only omittable field: it is ABSENT from the payload when no due date is set, never present-and-null. Test for presence, not for null. Millisecond precision: exactly three fractional-second digits, UTC. Every timestamp on this topic is normalised through getTime() on both publish paths, so the create path (Spanner commit response) and the update path (a PreciseDate read-back) cannot emit different widths. Sub-millisecond precision is dropped deliberately

modifiedDatetime.description: The record's own last-modified timestamp as of this publish (stock_count_business_units.modified_datetime), ISO 8601 UTC. Millisecond precision: exactly three fractional-second digits, UTC. Every timestamp on this topic is normalised through getTime() on both publish paths, so the create path (Spanner commit response) and the update path (a PreciseDate read-back) cannot emit different widths. Sub-millisecond precision is dropped deliberately. The producer's write time — not the publish time and not the delivery time. Use it to discard a replayed message older than state already applied
